title: Blessing's Recovery Story
excerpt: Eighteen months after she was forced to drop out, Blessing is back in school, top of her class in biology, and one year away from sitting her West African Senior School Certificate Examination.
body:
When we first met Blessing, she was 14 years old and selling bananas at a roadside stand outside Monrovia. Her father had grown ill the year before, and the family of seven could no longer cover the $50 per term that her secondary school required for tuition, uniforms, and books. She had been out of school for eleven months.

Today, eighteen months later, Blessing is back in the classroom. Her last term report listed her as first in her class in biology and second in mathematics. She has decided she wants to be a nurse.

What changed

Three things, in roughly this order:

  • A monthly sponsorship of $30 covered her tuition, uniform, and a bag of textbooks shared by no more than two other students.
  • A weekly check-in from a CECE coordinator made sure she had a quiet place to study and the kerosene she needed to read after dark.
  • Her father's medication was stabilized through a small grant from a partner clinic, which meant Blessing was no longer the family's primary income.

None of this is dramatic on its own. The drama is in the math: $30 a month, multiplied by twelve, is the difference between a girl who sells bananas and a girl who is one year away from sitting the West African Senior School Certificate Examination.

I want to take care of my mother and my sisters. I want them to know that what I am doing now is for them.

What's next

Blessing has one academic year left before her WASSCE exams. With strong scores she's eligible for nursing school in Monrovia, where CECE has standing relationships with two faculties that offer reduced-rate placements for sponsored students. We'll keep you updated.

title: Spring 2026 Impact Report
excerpt: This term we covered tuition for 87 students across three counties, distributed 412 textbooks, and supported the construction of a new latrine block at our partner school in Bomi.
body:
This term, your support reached further than any previous term in CECE's history. A short summary, by the numbers:

  • 87 students received full tuition coverage across Montserrado, Bomi, and Bong counties.
  • 412 textbooks were distributed, lowering the average student-to-textbook ratio at our partner schools from 22:1 to 8:1.
  • 1 new latrine block opened at our Bomi partner school, replacing a single shared pit latrine for 340 students.

Where the money went

For every dollar donated this term, 84 cents reached a school directly, 11 cents covered field staff and transport in Liberia, and 5 cents covered U.S. operations.

What we learned

Two things stood out. First: textbook distribution had a measurable effect on attendance. At schools where the student-to-textbook ratio dropped below 10:1, weekly attendance rose by an average of 9 percentage points. Second: the new latrine in Bomi corresponded with a sharper enrollment increase among girls than we expected — a reminder that infrastructure and gender outcomes are tightly linked.

Thank you for making this term possible.

title: Why We Don't Build Schools
excerpt: We get this question constantly: why doesn't CECE build new schools? The honest answer is that Liberia doesn't need more buildings. It needs more children inside the buildings that already exist.
body:
We get this question constantly, and we understand why. Building a school is concrete, photogenic, and easy to explain to a donor. Tuition assistance is none of those things.

But the honest answer is that Liberia doesn't need more buildings. It needs more children inside the buildings that already exist.

The data

According to the most recent EMIS census, Liberia has roughly 6,000 schools serving a school-age population of more than two million. Average primary school enrollment is 46% of the eligible age group. Average completion for primary school is 10%.

The bottleneck isn't classroom capacity. It's the gap between a family's daily survival income and the cost of a school term. Tuition, a uniform, and a bag of books costs roughly what a family earns in two months. So the children stay home, or they sell at the market, or they walk to school for a few weeks until the books run out.

What works instead

What works is removing that economic barrier for one child at a time. Cover tuition. Cover the uniform. Make sure books are in the bag. Then check in monthly to make sure the child is showing up, learning, and not being pulled back into the household economy.

The buildings are already there. The teachers are already there. What's missing is the affordability of the seat.

When we will build

There are two cases where we'd help fund construction: when an existing school's facilities are actively dangerous (collapsing roofs, no toilets, no clean water), or when a community of 500+ school-age children has no school within reasonable walking distance. We've done one of each in our history. Both were expensive, both were necessary, and neither was the highest-leverage use of donor money in any year.

Our default assumption is: don't build. Send the kids in.
